extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, epidemiologists, health technology assessment researchers and other researchers studying publication bias
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic review and meta-analysis assessing whether study results (e.g. statistically significant/important vs non-significant/non-important) are associated with subsequent publication, including definitions/classifications of results, methods for ascertaining publication, meta-analytic methods, and investigation of factors associated with publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of study results — Bardy (1998) scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Results classified as positive, inconclusive or negative: positive if the risk–benefit ratio was in favour of the drug or the objective of the study was supported; inconclusive if the risk–benefit assessment was inconclusive or the study was non-comparative; negative if the benefit–risk ratio was not in favour of the drug or no different from placebo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to categorise completed trials and compare rates of publication (example: publication rates 47% positive, 33% inconclusive, 11% negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance / 'showed (an) effect' definition (Cronin & Sheldon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies categorised as 'showed (an) effect' or not depending on whether results were statistically significant (p < 0.05) or considered to be of great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to dichotomise study findings when comparing publication rates (example comparison: 76% vs 64%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory / invalidating / inconclusive classification (Decullier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators classified results as confirmatory, invalidating or inconclusive; alternatively investigators subjectively rated importance on a 1–10 scale and defined 'important' as > 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare publication rates by degree of result importance (examples: OR = 4.59 for confirmatory vs inconclusive; 70% vs 60% publication for important vs less important).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant / non-significant / mixed (Misakian & Bero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study results classified as statistically significant, statistically non-significant, or mixed (mixed refers to a situation in which at least one of multiple primary outcomes was statistically significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied when multiple primary outcomes exist; publication rates reported separately for these categories (example: 85% significant, 86% non-significant, 14% mixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive / non-positive (abstracts; language-varying definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some studies (e.g. Zimpel and Windeler) used 'positive' vs 'non-positive' classifications; exact definitions may vary and can be language-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about local definitions and translation issues when using such dichotomies to compare publication rates (example: 40% positive vs 28% negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory classification (FDA/agency-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory studies classified trials according to regulatory authority decisions (e.g. Turner et al.: positive, questionable or negative according to the FDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory classification can differ from purely statistical definitions; examples show higher publication for trials deemed 'positive' by regulators (97% vs 33% negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance definition for meta-analyses (Lee et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical significance of the primary outcome defined as p < 0.05 or a confidence interval (CI) excluding no difference. For equivalency or non-inferiority trials, the statistically significant result refers to those with 'p > 0.05 or a CI including no difference or a CI excluding the pre-specified difference described in the trial'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rules for what counts as 'significant' in different trial designs are necessary when determining publication status by result; reported publication rates differed by significance (example: 66% vs 36%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'favourable'/'important' results for pooled inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: For pooled analyses a positive result was defined inclusively as important or confirmatory or significant; a 'non-positive' result included negative, non-important, inconclusive or non-significant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inclusive definition allowed combining heterogeneous cohort studies (inception, regulatory, abstract, manuscript) into pooled analyses; be explicit about definitions when broadening inclusion criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of cohort/study sources to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish cohort types: inception cohorts (follow-up of research protocols), regulatory cohorts (trials submitted to regulators), meeting-abstract cohorts (abstracts presented at meetings/journals followed for full publication), and manuscript cohorts (manuscripts submitted to journals and their acceptance/publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different cohort types have different biases and information availability; analyses are often stratified by cohort type (examples: pooled ORs reported separately for inception, regulatory, abstract and manuscript cohorts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to ascertain publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine publication by searching bibliographic databases (MEDLINE, PubMed, other databases) and by contacting authors, supervisors, companies, trial sponsors or regulatory authorities; use personal communication or interviews where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine database searches with direct contact to reduce misclassification of unpublished studies; several studies reported using both approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication outcome metric — formal publication and publication types
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome measured as rate of formal publication (percent published) and as odds ratios (OR) comparing publication of studies with positive vs non-positive results; formal publication includes stand-alone, pooled or multiple publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both absolute publication rates and relative measures (OR with 95% CI) and be explicit about what constitutes 'formal publication'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analytic methods and heterogeneity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Association between study results and publication measured using odds ratios (OR); heterogeneity across studies measured using the I2 statistic; meta-analyses used a random-effects model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report I2 and p-values for heterogeneity; use random-effects pooling when heterogeneity is expected; e.g. I2 = 61% (p = 0.05) for inception subgroup in this review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of funnel-plot asymmetry (publication bias diagnostics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct funnel plots by subgroup and test asymmetry using the method recommended by Peters et al.: linear regression with log odds ratio as the dependent variable and the inverse of the total sample size as the independent variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report p-values for asymmetry tests for each subgroup; in this review no statistically significant asymmetry was found for inception, regulatory, abstract or manuscript subgroups using Peters' method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup and sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform subgroup analyses (e.g. restrict to clinical trials, examine levels of evidence) and sensitivity analyses (e.g. exclude outlier studies) to explore heterogeneity and robustness of pooled estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: excluding Misakian and Bero from inception cohorts changed pooled OR; restricting to clinical trials produced similar conclusions but fewer included cohorts. Report subgroup-specific pooled ORs and heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to investigate as potential predictors of publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate study-level factors such as study design (observational, laboratory-based experimental, non-randomised trials vs RCTs), type of study, single vs multicentre, sample size thresholds (e.g. ≥100 or >20), funding source, investigators' characteristics (gender, degree, academic rank), use of randomisation/blinding, and having a comparison group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report associations (or lack thereof) between these factors and publication rates; prior findings: observational/lab/non-randomised trials had greater risk than RCTs, concurrent comparison group and larger sample size associated with less bias in some analyses, but many factors showed no consistent association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of manuscript-cohort designs relating to editor influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript cohort studies often require editor support or collaboration; in prospective studies editors' awareness of the ongoing study may influence acceptance decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge potential bias introduced by editorial cooperation and awareness when interpreting results from manuscript cohorts; treat findings with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-publication as an outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Time to publication can be examined in accepted manuscripts and compared by result significance (example: median times 7.8 months for positive vs 7.6 months for negative; p = 0.44).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time-to-event analyses where appropriate to assess whether statistically significant results are published faster; report median times and p-values or hazard ratios.
